snap verdict6h agoBurnham describes Tory MPs as pro-Brexit 'zombies'6h agoBurnham and Badenoch clash over welfare6h agoBurnham faces Badenoch at PMQs7h agoYvette Cooper announces new health support for most vulnerable people in England7h agoLammy claims 'many' Tory voters could switch to Labour at next election if party committed to rejoining EU7h agoMahmood to tell police chiefs that leadership is ‘frankly inadequate’8h agoTories and Reform UK dismiss Mahmood's bid to assuage concerns about 'two-tier policing'8h agoLucy Powell criticises media organisations for playing prison message from Russell Brand8h agoBurnham considering cuts to national insurance to create more youth jobs8h agoLammy rules out standing to be Labour's next candidate for London mayor8h agoLammy says he doesn't think there is two-tier policing in Britain, but he supports 'tidying up' guidance on this9h agoLammy says Burnham should put rejoining EU in Labour's next manifesto9h agoEnergy bills in Great Britain forecast to rise by 26% to £2,166 from January9h agoMahmood to tell the police 'leave politics to the politicians'9h agoShabana Mahmood pledges to tackle ‘corrosive and growing perception of two-tier policing’1h ago17.06 GMTAfternoon summary Andy Burnham has said that Kemi Badenoch should withdraw her “crass and insensitive” comment justifying cuts to disability benefits on the grounds that “double amputees run marathons”. (See 2.35pm.)

Andy Burnham should fight the next election on a promise to rejoin the EU, the former business secretary Peter Kyle has said, with voters given a referendum on the outcome of any deal.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, has been dealt a double blow after two UK companies signalled plans to pull their investment from large fossil fuel projects amid disagreements over government policies.

Half a million of the most vulnerable people in England will get proactive help with their health needs from new teams that will act as a “downpayment” on the promised national care service, Yvette Cooper has announced.

Labour’s Brussels talks will be a “gold-winning failure” which will sign away British sovereignty, the Tories have said. As the Press Association reports, shadow Cabinet Office minister Mike Wood accused Downing Street of having been a “docile negotiating partner” in negotiations during a Commons debate on a Conservative party motion attacking most aspects of the proposed deal. But the Foreign Office minister Hamish Falconer said he was “confident” the outcome would “deliver a better deal for those who voted Brexit and the like”. MPs are voting now. The Tory motion won’t pass, but it is worth recording because it sets out the party’s official stance on the renegotiation. It says:

double quotation markThat this house believes that taxes, regulations governing product and food standards, and migration policies should be set by the UK parliament, not the European Union; further believes that giving the EU control over these matters will lead to more expensive goods for British citizens and increased costs and regulations on businesses; also believes that UK taxpayers should not be paying to subsidise university fees for EU students at all, particularly while the government refuses to take action to reduce the cost of plan 2 student loans for British students; and believes that UK taxpayers should not have to pay any additional money to the EU.

View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham at PMQs. Photograph: House of Commons/PAShare2h ago16.41 GMTZia Yusuf claims ex-Tory MPs now in Reform UK banned from involvement in its immigration or borders policyBen QuinnBen Quinn is a Guardian political correspondent.

Former Conservative defectors to Reform UK have been barred from shaping the party’s immigration policy, its home affairs spokesman has claimed, effectively excluding the majority of its MPs.

The comments were made by Zia Yusuf, who was previously embroiled in a bitter feud with Robert Jenrick before the former Tory minister made the jump to Nigel Farage’s party earlier this year to become its self-styled ‘shadow chancellor’.

“I don’t think the country has time for us to not be candid about these things,” Yusuf told a podcast by the Spectator magazine when asked about the potential role in Reform of former Conservatives who had served in governments which did not bring migration numbers down.

“So if you are in the category of being concerned about [former Conservatives being involved in Reform], none of the above are going to be involved in immigration policy or borders policy,” he said.

“There’s a reason why Nigel’s given me this brief and not them,” he told the Spectator editor and former Conservative minister, Michael Gove.

Yusuf, who added that he had felt “personally” betrayed by Boris Johnson’s government as a Conservative voter, went on to qualify his comments by saying that Suella Braverman, a former home secretary, and Robert Jenrick, a former immigration minister, had either been sacked or resigned “over immigration policy or issues around culture.”

Nevertheless, the comments once again raise questions about unity at the very top of Reform and, in particular, the attitude of Yusuf, who has been the frontline Reform figure who has been most hostile towards the Conservatives.

Both Braverman, officially Reform’s education spokesperson, and Jenrick have continued to wade into immigration and cultural issues. The claims that former Tories have no role in immigration policy for Reform also appear to be at odds with, for example, Jenrick’s announcement in June of plans for a migrant labour levy.

He and Braverman make up five of Reform’s eight MPs, while a range of former Conservative MPs have joined the party. They include the former chancellor Nadhim Zahawi, former Conservative party chairman Jake Berry and former ministers Nadine Dorries and Andrea Jenkyns.

A number of former Tory MPs have also jumped to Reform including Ben Bradley, who is now head of local government at Reform HQ.

Suspicion of those defectors has long cut through Reform’s own grassroots, with Yusuf becoming a voice for them. Farage himself has frequently had to push back against claims that his party had become “the Conservative party 2.0”, and said in January that Reform would not accept any more defectors after local elections were held on 7 May.

double quotation markThe people of Piddington, Oxfordshire, voted in September to secede from the UK after the government announced plans to house 1,256 male asylum seekers at a nearby former military base. Communities secretary Angela Rayner has since approved full planning permission for MoD Bicester to be used for housing asylum seekers. Barnham in Suffolk is to hold a similar Yes/No poll on Saturday, asking residents whether they support a petition for “crown dependency status”. It comes as there is a proposal to house 931 asylum seekers at RAF Barnham. John Bauer, chairman of Barnham parish council, said the independence referendum has been organised by Barnham residents’ association. He said people will vote on whether they support a petition for “crown dependency status” and described this as “a bit like Jersey, Guernsey, Isle of Man whereby we retain loyalty to the crown yet while still removing ourselves from the Home Office jurisdiction”. The symbolic vote will carry no legal weight. Asked what he hopes it will achieve, Bauer said: “It’s to express the concern of the village at the way we’re not being consulted, the treatment by the Home Office, the whole thing, we feel we’re being totally ignored.”

Read moreShare2h ago16.06 GMTPolice unions criticise Home Office plan to fast-track recruits into leadership rolesPolice unions have criticised the plan announced by the Home Office today to fast-track recruits into leadership positions. (See 10.57am.)

Under the plan, up to 200 recruits per year will join a scheme that could allow them to become a superintendent in five to 10 years.

Nick Smart, president of the Police Superintendents’ Association, said:

double quotation markIt is extremely disappointing that an announcement of this significance has been made without detail or meaningful consultation with the workforce. Our most recent member survey found that 88% of respondents believe the government does not value policing as highly as other public services. The lack of meaningful consultation on significant proposals such as this only serves to reinforce those concerns. Policing already has huge talent within its ranks, and any fast-track system must provide fair and equitable opportunities for those officers, while ensuring leaders have the operational credibility required at superintendent level. Previous direct entry to superintendent schemes saw limited take-up from forces, with the majority not choosing to use them, so government must explain what will be different this time.

And Paul Williams, acting national chairman of the Police Federation, that represents officers from the rank of constable to chief inspector, said:

double quotation markAt five years’ service, more officers are thinking about leaving policing before it breaks them than they are becoming a superintendent. Policing cannot fast-track its way to credible leadership while ignoring the fundamentals: pay, training, unsustainable workloads and exploitative working conditions that are driving too many experienced and credible future leaders out of the job.

Read moreShare3h ago15.47 GMTMahmood amends speech to NPCC conference to make it clear she thinks two-tier policing claims 'false'As reported earlier (see 9.04am), the Home Office released overnight extracts from the speech Shabana Mahmood was giving this afternoon covering so-called two-tier policing. Journalists were told Mahmood would say:

double quotation markWe must tackle head-on the corrosive and growing perception of two-tier policing in this country … There have been examples of differential treatment and they have harmed policing, allowing people – often motivated actors – to whip up the idea that there is two-tier policing in this country.

This quote did not make it clear whether Mahmood thought the perception of two-tier policing was true, false, of whether it was somewhere in between. At the post-PMQs lobby briefing, asked if the perception was a false one, No 10 sidestepped the question and just said it was a perception.

But, when Mahmood delivered her speech, she added the word “false” to her text to make it clear that she believes two-tier policing allegations are unfounded. She said:

double quotation markI know the vast majority of officers police impartially and that policing without fear or favour is their creed. But there have been examples of differential treatment and they have harmed policing, allowing some to whip up the false idea that there is two-tier policing in this country.

The full text of her speech is here.

Speaking to reporters after delivering her speech, Mahmood said:

double quotation markWhat Reform and others will have you believe is every single day officers go out and they practice a thing called two-tier policing. That is utter, complete, ridiculous rubbish. That is not what’s happening in our police forces. But there have been examples of differential treatment, and those have had an impact on confidence in policing, and they’ve allowed that false perception of two-tier policing to take hold.

Photograph: Will Colebourne/PAShare3h ago15.12 GMTHome Office says policing in England and Wales to be based on 200 'local commands' as part of biggest reforms since 1800sPolicing in England and Wales will be restructured into about 200 local commands, Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, has said.

Under what the Home Office claims will be “the biggest reforms to policing in 200 years”, the government will set up around 200 new “local police commands” (LPCs). They will deal with routine crime like burglary, vehicle theft and antisocial behaviour.

Announcing the changes, the Home Office said:

double quotation markSince the government unveiled plans in January to fundamentally restructure the policing model, much focus has been on reducing the number of forces at a regional level. However, delivering a keynote speech to police leaders today, Shabana Mahmood announced she will build a structure from the bottom up with a larger number of smaller commands that will focus solely on the needs of their local area. LPCs will be the foundation of the new policing model, focused on keeping neighbourhoods safe and tackling crimes like burglary, vehicle theft, phone theft and antisocial behaviour. Each one will be situated closer to the areas they serve, with decision making driven by local knowledge and understanding. Broadly aligned to the geographical boundaries of councils, LPCs will cover towns or rural areas. This will also allow police to work in closer partnership with other local services such as probation, health and housing and improve outcomes. A new local police guarantee will ensure every LPC delivers the same high-quality local policing, no matter where in the country they serve.

The Home Office said that this move would be the first step towards a wider programme of police reform. There are 43 police forces in England and Wales and in January Mahmood published a white paper setting out plans for some of them to be merged. The Home Office has been looking at plans for a much smaller number of regional police forces, but progress has been held up because how these would fit alongside Andy Burnham’s plans to give mayoral authorities more say over policing remains unresolved.

The Home Office news release suggests LPCs will be at the bottom of the policing pyramid, and the National Police Service at the top. It does not say what happens in between.

double quotation markEvery LPC will have a named commander, accountable to their local community and elected officials, with communities able to have a role in setting their local priorities. Above them will sit specialist services that will lead investigations on the most serious and complex crimes. They will be responsible for delivering specialist functions such as public order, forensics and firearms. This will guarantee that no matter where anyone is, they will have access to expert specialist policing which the current system does not provide. The new system will also remove the administrative duplication that exists across the existing 43 police headquarters, freeing up thousands of police officers to return to neighbourhood policing. The final structure within policing would be the National Police Service which will tackle nationwide and international threats. It will bring together the world-leading capabilities of Counter Terrorism Policing and other agencies, ensuring that policing has the technology, intelligence and resources needed to tackle crime in the 21st century.

Updated at 15.13 GMT4h ago14.35 GMTBurnham says Badenoch should withdraw 'crass' comment defending disability cuts on grounds 'amputees run marathons'Andy Burnham has said that Kemi Badenoch should withdraw her “crass and insensitive” comment justifying cuts to disability benefits on the grounds that “double amputees run marathons”.

After Badenoch used this line in a speech last week, the Paralympian Richard Whitehead posted a message on Facebook criticising her. He said:

double quotation markDisability should never be judged through isolated examples of individual achievement, but through an understanding of the barriers people and families face every day. The fact that some double-leg amputees can run marathons does not mean that disability support is unnecessary. Equally, the fact that some people with ADHD thrive despite limited support does not mean that others do not need meaningful assistance.

In subsequent remarks, Whitehead said that Badenoch’s comments were “divisive” and that he was “gobsmacked that somebody’s sporting success would be weaponised in this way”.

Read moreAt PMQs today, the Labour MP Charlotte Nichols asked Burnham whether he agreed with Whitehead that “the achievements of our sports men and women with disabilities should never be weaponised against others”.

double quotation markI thought the comments by Richard Whitehead do deserve a response from the right honourable lady [Badenoch]. They were crass and insensitive, and I think she should withdraw them.

Whitehead has run more than 100 marathons, set world records and won four Paralympic medals.

Photograph: HoCShareUpdated at 14.39 GMT5h ago13.42 GMTPMQs - snap verdictGuardian readers probably don’t need much persuading that PMQs is a terrible forum for reasonable debate, and there was a good example today that shows why. In his final response to Kemi Badenoch, Burnham accused her of adopting a “patronising tone”. This was uncharacteristically personal, and it lit up on social media as about the most interesting line from the exchange, with some commentators implying it was a gaffe. In reality, of course, it was probably one of the least contentious things Burnham said. Badenoch is patronising, particularly at PMQs. If there were a world championships for being patronising, she would be leading the UK team. Yet Burnham will probably conclude that it was a mistake, and something he shouldn’t have said.

Why? Because it made him look a bit rattled. Burnham came into office determined to pursue “problem solving, not point scoring”, but increasingly that is looking like a lost cause and the centrifugal power of PMQs yanks him back into a slanging match. (He is not always like this with opposition backbenchers, but he is – inevitably – with Badenoch.) Today, speaking to the Tory leader, he seemed to devote more time than ever to attacking her party’s record, rather than seeking common ground. On the plus side, the points he was making about the Conservatives’ record, and about her policy agenda now consisting of little more than welfare cuts, were forceful. On the negative side, he sounded like someone on the defensive.

Just as she did last week, Badenoch was reasonably good at delivering the sort of broad-brush ‘You’re rubbish’ messaging that would work as a headline for a Daily Express op ed. But it was hard to discern what particular attack line she wanted to land. There was a time when she would arrive at PMQs with a pre-prepared gotcha question and afterwards, normally following Keir Starmer’s refusal to answer, CCHQ would send out a press release highlighting the alleged implications of the question-dodging. There was none of that today, or last week.

One of Badenoch’s most interesting claims was that Burnham is just offering the “vibes” of welfare reform, not the real thing. But that claim is so wide of the mark it is unlikely to work even with a Tory audience. The Milburn plan may have its drawbacks, but it is absurd to dismiss it as just vibes.

Sky News also set Badenoch up for another attack, highlighting Alan Milburn saying yesterday that some people would lose from the reforms, while Burnham said in a separate interview he did not want anyone to lose out. It was a classic case of apples and pears; Milburn was saying people will lose out from the benefit cuts, while Burnham was saying that, because those cuts are part of a strategy intended to divert off benefits into work, in the long run they wouldn’t lose out. Mindful, perhaps, of the ‘if you’re explaining, you’re losing’ theory of political communications, Burnham did not want to clarify this, and he just sidestepped her question. Badenoch then did not pursue the point, which was strange because a follow-up question could have made it much more awkward for him.

Burnham says there was action in the Employment Rights Act to tackle this, but the government could go further, he says. He says they will look to see if this can be extended to freelancers.

Burnham says he does not know the details. This sounds like an issue for the Tories, he says. But he says he will arrange a meeting for Khan about this.

Updated at 14.17 GMT6h ago12.41 GMTAndrew George (Lib Dem) says the budget will reward second home owners who let their homes. They will get a tax benefit. This is public money that could be better spent helping people in housing need.

And he says he was disappointed his private member’s bill on this did not get government support.

Burnham says he asked officials to look seriously at the bill. “It was felt that it wasn’t the best way to address the issues, but we don’t disagree with what he’s trying to do,” he says. He says he will arrange for the housing minister to meet George.

Burnham says the government has been “relentless in tackling violence against women and girls in every single respect”. He says he is not aware of this issue, but will look into it.
